properties.name: Addicks Estates
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — UNDERCOUNTED COMMUNITY: Addicks Estates residents live east of I-495, directly adjacent to the Citisteel contamination site (343 acres), I-495, and the new transit center. But their census block group extends north all the way to the PA border, swallowing the entire uninhabited industrial waterfront along the Delaware River. This dilutes the pollution burden score and caused DelDOT to miss this neighborhood in the EFA designation entirely. Real cumulative burden is likely much higher than scores shown. CC4EJ position: Addicks Estates warrants its own census block group for accurate EJ assessment. This gap should be raised in any DNREC permit review affecting this area.

properties.name: Aniline Village
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — UNDERCOUNTED COMMUNITY: Aniline Village has a large Spanish-speaking population whose linguistic isolation burden is being hidden by a census block group that also includes Hickman Road and Knollwood/Worthland — three distinct neighborhoods with different demographics lumped together. Linguistic isolation is a key EJScreen vulnerability indicator: communities where residents speak limited English have reduced ability to participate in permit hearings, access health information, and advocate for themselves. By averaging Aniline Village's Spanish-speaking residents across a broader block group, the linguistic isolation score is diluted and DNREC's permit review tools systematically undercount this community's vulnerability. CC4EJ position: Aniline Village, Knollwood, and Hickman Rd warrant separate census block group designations.

properties.name: Hickman Road
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — NATIONAL REGISTER OF HISTORIC PLACES (2006): Hickman Row was built around 1919 by Worth Steel Corporation to house its Black workforce. Residents were families from the Great Migration — people who fled Southern racism seeking economic opportunity and a new life in industrial Delaware. The neighborhood's back lots were large enough to raise vegetables and livestock. When Worth Steel sold the properties in 1962, many African American families stayed and continued building community here. Today Hickman Row sits in the same census block group as Aniline Village and Knollwood/Worthland — three communities with distinct histories, demographics, and pollution exposures averaged into a single number. A community that survived the Great Migration and a century of industrial neighbors deserves to be counted accurately. CC4EJ position: Hickman Road warrants its own census block group designation. Historical marker NC-162, Delaware State Archives.

properties.name: Knollwood / Worthland
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — UNDERCOUNTED COMMUNITY: Knollwood (also known as Worthland) has a significant Spanish-speaking population that shares a census block group with Hickman Road and Aniline Village — masking the distinct demographics and cumulative burdens of each neighborhood. This boundary failure means linguistic isolation, income, and pollution exposure data are averaged across communities that have little in common geographically or demographically. A community where residents cannot easily read permit notices or attend English-only hearings faces a compounded barrier to environmental protection. CC4EJ position: this block group should be split to accurately represent these three distinct neighborhoods.
